ALEXIS WEAVER.name: Alexis Weaver
ALEXIS WEAVER.background: Tucker (DeKalb County) resident; urban planner and nonprofit leader with about two decades in community and economic development, including five years at a chamber of commerce; Run for Something's profile describes her as a senior manager at Atlanta's food bank and a board member of Tucker's largest local social service nonprofit. ALEXIS WEAVER.ideology: Nonpartisan office. Listed with a 2021 endorsement in the Run for Something candidate directory; her 2021 platform centered on a non-discrimination ordinance protecting LGBTQ residents and opposing the criminalization of homelessness.
ALEXIS WEAVER.record: Says she helped pass Tucker's non-discrimination ordinance protecting LGBTQ residents, led the effort to make Juneteenth a city holiday, pushed for a homelessness and mental-health coordinator position, and cites the 2023 Housing Study and the inclusion of bikeways in SPLOST II.
ALEXIS WEAVER.notes: Rechecked 2026-11-05. Rebuilt from her campaign site, Rough Draft Atlanta (2025) and Decaturish (2021) Q&As, and the Run for Something directory. The 2025 opponent, Sam Ulrich, is named in the Rough Draft headline. The education details in the old profile (Baylor, UT) were not on any opened page and are dropped.

positions.stance: "The number-one topic I hear about is housing." Wants a mix of housing for seniors, people with disabilities and average-income workers while preserving neighborhood character; supports joining the DeKalb County regional land bank to redevelop abandoned properties.

Ran in 2021 because "I couldn't stay silent when our city passed an urban camping ban that criminalized people simply for being unhoused"; pushed for a homelessness and mental-health coordinator position.
Strong supporter in 2021, calling the council's unwillingness to discuss one "a glaring failure"; says she helped pass it in her first term.

Prioritizes tree canopy protection and safer routes for cyclists and pedestrians; cites including bikeways in the SPLOST II referendum. In 2021 called for more sidewalks, lighted crosswalks, bike lanes and traffic calming, and connecting Tucker to the PATH trail system.
"Taxpayer dollars should be spent with care and clarity."

Backs upgrades to roads, sidewalks and stormwater systems that "truly improve daily life"; in 2021 wanted a feasibility study and community input before Tucker takes over roads and drainage from DeKalb.
In 2021 supported promoting masks and vaccines, including requiring masks at city facilities and indoor events.
In 2021 proposed citizen advisory boards, including one on diversity and inclusion, and an equity assessment of city activities.

statements.text: "Tucker is at a turning point."
Endorsed Robin Biro for mayor, saying it was time for new leadership after Mayor Auman's two terms.

ALISON COUCH.name: Alison Couch
ALISON COUCH.background: Ran as a Republican in the partisan races on record. In the November 3, 2026 general election (count not yet certified), led in the race for County Commission Chairperson, Columbia County.

positions.stance: Committed to pursuing property-tax relief for homeowners, managing growth to reduce burden, using growth to lower tax burden, focused on fiscal discipline and lower taxes, would reduce county government portion of property taxes.
q: I’m committed to pursuing meaningful property-tax relief for Columbia County homeowners.
By managing growth responsibly, expanding our tax base, and protecting taxpayer dollars, we can reduce the burden on families while maintaining the services our community relies on.

positions.stance: Would focus on maintaining public safety, affordability, neighborhoods and development with adequate infrastructure, continue investing in law enforcement, fire and emergency services as population grows, supports first responders and keeps communities safe as they grow, supports investments for first responders and public-safety professionals, supported leadership during the storm by listening, solving problems and working with responders.
q: Alison’s approach would focus on maintaining strong public safety, keeping the county affordable, protecting established neighborhoods and rural areas, and ensuring that development is supported by adequate roads, services and infrastructure.
Continue investing in law enforcement, fire and emergency services as the county’s population grows.

positions.stance: Has worked to protect taxpayers, strengthen public safety, improve infrastructure, ensure responsible growth, advocated for small businesses, brought fiscally responsible approach to county government, and would prioritize economic development that broadens tax base and creates quality jobs.
q: As a small-business owner, accountant, and current County Commissioner, I have worked to protect taxpayers, strengthen public safety, improve infrastructure, and ensure our growth is managed responsibly.

Alison’s advocacy for small businesses has taken her to Washington, where she has testified before the U.S. House Committee on Ways & Means, giving Georgia business owners a voice in national policy discussions.

positions.stance: Supports maintaining and expanding parks, recreation, public spaces and community amenities, modernizing older parks and planning new amenities for growing areas, a network of multi-use and golf-cart connections linking neighborhoods with parks and amenities, and investments in Parks & Recreation.
q: Maintain and expand the parks, recreation opportunities, public spaces and community amenities residents use every day.

Columbia County’s parks are an important part of its quality of life, and Alison’s priorities include continuing to modernize older facilities while planning new amenities for growing areas of the county.

positions.stance: Believed county needed to act before development occurred, supported White Oak Industrial Park while voting against proposals at Pumpkin Center and Byrd property, and believes county should take approach of setting high standards, protecting residents, and pursuing economic development with measurable community benefit.
q: As data-center developers began considering Columbia County, Alison believed the county needed to act before development occurred, rather than waiting for problems to arise.

Of three major data-center rezoning proposals considered by the Commission, Alison supported the White Oak Industrial Park location while voting against proposals at Pumpkin Center and the Byrd property.

positions.stance: Prioritizes preserving quality of life while addressing growth realities, supports maintaining desirable qualities and opposes proposals not judged based on their impact on residents.
q: As Commission Chair, Alison Couch’s stated priorities center on preserving Columbia County’s quality of life while addressing the realities that come with continued growth—from taxes and public safety to infrastructure, recreation and the appearance of the community.
Growth should not mean losing the qualities that made Columbia County a desirable place to live in the first place.

positions.stance: Supports White Oak data center for meeting strict standards and providing property-tax relief and says the project was paired with commitments to ensure energy infrastructure costs are borne by the end user rather than local ratepayers.
q: I supported the White Oak data center because it met strict standards and could provide meaningful property-tax relief.

The White Oak project was ultimately paired with commitments from Google and Georgia Power designed to ensure the project's energy infrastructure costs are borne by the end user rather than local ratepayers.

positions.stance: Provides oversight of county finances, operations and internal controls and supports good government that listens, spends responsibly and produces results.
q: As Chair of the Commission's Audit Committee and Management & Internal Services Committee, Alison provides direct oversight of county finances, operations and internal controls, helping ensure taxpayers' dollars are managed responsibly.
Her record reflects a simple belief: good government should listen carefully, spend responsibly and produce results that improve the everyday lives of the people it serves.

positions.stance: Supports growth accompanied by roads, water, sewer and public infrastructure and would explore transportation planning beyond adding more road lanes.
q: Her focus remains clear: growth must be accompanied by the roads, water, sewer and public infrastructure necessary to support it.
Transportation planning does not have to begin and end with adding more lanes to roads.

positions.stance: Would maintain community where families get value for taxes paid, including good roads and services.
q: Alison’s priorities would include maintaining a community where families receive meaningful value for the taxes and fees they pay, including good roads, quality parks, reliable public services, safe neighborhoods and amenities that improve everyday life.
